questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the key difference between 'profiling' and 'defining' a data quality rule?
options: Profiling describes what the data actually contains without judgment; defining decides whether that's acceptable
Profiling and defining are two names for the exact same activity
Defining always happens before profiling in the lifecycle
Profiling is only used for financial data, defining for all other data
questions.explain: Profiling is discovery (e.g. 'this column is 3% NULL'); defining is the judgment call, made in the define stage, about whether that rate is acceptable.

questions.q: A table shows up in SSMS's Object Explorer. What does that confirm, per this lesson?
options: Only that the table exists — it says nothing about whether the data inside it is good
That every column in the table has already been profiled
That the table has zero NULL values
That the data has passed all data quality checks
questions.explain: Object Explorer tells you what tables exist; profiling queries tell you what's actually inside them — the lesson is explicit that these are not the same thing.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of relationship profiling, per this lesson's three levels?
options: Checking whether foreign keys between two tables actually match up and whether any rows are orphaned
Counting how many rows in a single column are NULL
Finding the minimum and maximum value in a numeric column
Checking whether a phone column's values all match an expected format
questions.explain: Relationship profiling looks across tables for things like mismatched or orphaned foreign keys; the phone-format example is pattern profiling instead.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in this lesson as one of the core profiling metrics?
options: Average customer satisfaction score
Row count
NULL count / rate
Distinct count
questions.explain: The five core metrics named are row count, NULL count/rate, distinct count, min/max, and pattern/format breakdown — customer satisfaction isn't a profiling metric.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue it's worth learning profiling vocabulary (column, relationship, pattern) before writing any SQL?
options: So that when real T-SQL profiling queries appear in Lesson 7, you recognize what each one is doing and why, instead of just copying syntax
Because SQL Server will not execute a query without this vocabulary being defined first
Because SSMS requires selecting a profiling level from a menu before running any query
Because the vocabulary is tested separately from the rest of the course
questions.explain: The lesson's stated goal is building understanding first so the SQL in Lesson 7 is meaningful rather than memorized syntax.
